claims.text: A critical Si content in CrFeCoNiSi promotes Si segregation to the metal–oxide interface during high-temperature exposure.
Interfacial Si segregation produces a continuous Si-enriched mixed oxide scale composed primarily of SiO2 and Cr2O3.
The SiO2–Cr2O3 mixed scale accommodates thermal-expansion mismatch and minimizes interfacial stress.
Reducing interfacial stress makes the oxide scale coherent and resistant to cracking and spallation.
CrFeCoNiSi alloys containing 5–10 at.% Si can be prepared in a single-phase metallic solid-solution state.
Systematically changing Si content will alter oxidation behavior relative to alloys in which Mn or Al replaces Si.
Oxidation behavior is to be compared in air at 950 °C for 100 hours.
A continuous SiO2 phase integrated with Cr2O3 relieves interfacial strain.
During high-temperature oxidation, Si preferentially segregates to the alloy surface.
Segregated Si reacts with oxygen to form a thin, continuous SiO2 phase.
The continuous SiO2 phase reduces oxygen diffusivity through the oxide scale.
The continuous SiO2 phase reduces thermally induced misfit stress at the oxide–metal interface.
CrFeCoNi-based alloys lacking sufficient Si develop oxide layers with higher mismatch stress.
Higher oxide–metal mismatch stress causes cracking and spallation.
An optimized Si content will yield a more coherent, adherent, and uniform oxide scale with less cracking and spallation than Mn- or Al-containing controls.
Mn- or Al-containing baseline alloys form less protective and more discontinuous oxide scales with greater interfacial stress under identical exposure conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase metallic solid-solution high-entropy alloys in air above 900 °C.
The critical Si content may depend on interactions with the other alloying elements.
Synthesis-dependent microstructural variation may affect oxide-scale formation and integrity.
